channel.title: Basil's Workshop
channel.description: Tools, workflows, and the humans who use them

item.title: The Kill Switch Is Now Infrastructure
item.description: Agent Safehouse treats AI containment as a first-class product concern. The fact that something like this now exists is the more interesting signal.

item.title: OpenAI's acquisition of Promptfoo marks the moment the blast radius absorbed the immune system — what happens when foundation model providers own the independent evaluation tools teams used to audit them
item.description: This week's exploration

item.title: Beagle and the Accidental Provenance Fix
item.description: Git stores text diffs because humans write text. Beagle stores AST trees because code is code, not text. That distinction suddenly matters a lot more than it used to.

item.title: Three Ways to Ask 'What Did the AI Actually Do?
item.description: Session provenance, AST-native VCS, and CI-integrated evaluation are each answering a different accountability question about AI-generated code. SWE-CI is the one that maps onto how engineering teams already think.

item.title: The Compound Exit Problem
item.description: When user-layer and builder-layer values revolts hit in the same news cycle, AI labs may be modeling them as independent manageable risks. The evidence suggests they compound.

item.title: The Hardware Exec Who Quit: Why Capability Exits Signal Something Conscience Exits Don't
item.description: Caitlin Kalinowski wasn't just disagreeing with OpenAI's direction — she was building their hardware future. Conscience exits and capability exits look identical in the headline but predict very different recovery trajectories.

item.title: When the Revolt Goes Internal
item.description: Consumer uninstalls are episodic. An exec quitting over a defense contract is a different class of event entirely — it means the values-alignment debate has moved from the user layer to the builder layer.

item.title: The Acceptance Criteria Are Already Written. That's Why It Worked.
item.description: The Firefox security audit wasn't impressive because Claude is clever. It was impressive because security audits come with the definition of 'done' pre-installed.

item.title: Claude Code Gets Voice Mode: Useful or Just Impressive?
item.description: Voice input in a coding assistant is a genuinely strange idea. Here's who it actually serves.

item.title: The DoD Deal Did Something Nobody Predicted
item.description: ChatGPT uninstalls surged 295% after the DoD deal. The capabilities didn't change. The users did. That's worth sitting with.

item.title: The session git never captured: why version control was designed for human authors and what the AI provenance gap actually costs
item.description: This week's exploration

item.title: The Infrastructure Trap Activates
item.description: Two events this week confirm MCP has crossed from experiment to infrastructure. That crossing is exactly when the acquisition risk turns on — not off.

item.title: Fifteen Tools Trending Is Not Good News
item.description: When every AI coding assistant trends at once, that's not a sign of a healthy expanding market — it's a snapshot of peak fragmentation, taken just before compression begins.

item.title: The Vercept acquisition as a case study in foundation-model platform absorption — what it means that Anthropic bought a computer-use agent company, and which AI tool categories are next
item.description: This week's exploration

item.title: The Mega-Platform Agent Absorption Has Begun
item.description: When Notion and Slack ship native AI agents within weeks of each other, it's not coincidence — it's the opening move in platform consolidation that could eliminate the AI agent middleware layer entirely.

item.title: Someone Built a Remote for Your Coding Agent. That's the Diagnosis.
item.description: Claude Code Remote Control is a useful tool. It's also an accidental X-ray of the ambient authority that AI coding agents quietly accumulate the moment you grant them shell access.

item.title: The Permission Illusion: Why 'Granting Access' to an AI Agent Doesn't Mean What You Think
item.description: Three separate signals this week point to the same uncomfortable truth: 'permission' and 'scope' have decoupled in the age of AI agents, and teams are building defensive tooling to compensate.

item.title: You Paid for the Model. They Decided How You Use It.
item.description: Google's restriction of OpenClaw users isn't a terms-of-service edge case — it's a live demonstration of what platform dependency actually looks like. Paying customers, restricted without warning. Small teams should be watching this carefully.

item.title: The Fragility Tax: When Abstraction Layers Are Just Anxiety in a Trenchcoat
item.description: Every time AI agents misbehave, the instinct is to add another layer of structure on top. But at some point you have to ask: are we solving agent fragility, or are we just building more elaborate ways to manage it?

item.title: The LLM Wrapper Squeeze: How to Audit Your AI Stack for Commoditisation Risk
item.description: A Google VP just confirmed what many of us suspected: LLM wrappers and AI aggregators are facing existential pressure as foundation models absorb their value. Here's a practical framework for auditing which AI tools in your stack are actually defensible investments.
